text: Alaska midterm race could be called on Wednesday as Peltola remains ahead of Republican incumbent
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
The final Senate race of this year’s midterm elections could be resolved tomorrow if Alaska election officials run the state’s ranked choice voting system to determine the result.

With 98% of ballots counted, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is out in front with 49.98% of the vote. By contrast, incumbent Republican senator Dan S Sullivan has a 45.93% share, according to the latest Associated Press figures.

In terms of actual voting numbers, Peltola is ahead by just over 11,000, with 141,637 compared to Sullivan’s 130,162. All eyes will be on Peltola to see if she can keep the pace to achieve 50% of the ballot, two weeks on from the election.
If not, then voters’ second choice votes will be counted. The outcome will determine the final balance of power in the chamber for the next two years, with Democrats already holding a 55-44 majority.

It comes in a turbulent Alaska race, which has seen president Trump demand that Peltola be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Piling on, Alaska’s Republican governor has since ordered an investigation into Peltola’s campaign.

A New York Times investigation reported that operatives working with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit another Dan Sullivan – Dan J Sullivan – a retired teacher from Petersburg, to split the incumbent’s vote. Peltola and her campaign have denied this.

The ‘other’ Sullivan, who stood as an independent candidate, has only received 4,684 votes – a 1.65% share – and is looking unlikely to be the cause of the Republican senator’s failure should he not retain his seat.

Elsewhere, president Trump has arrived in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, where he is due to meet south east Asian leaders and take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

In other developments:

Donald Trump defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after treasury secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that he has been pushing “for months” to add Megaspeed, the data center company led by an alleged Chinese spy who was reportedly in a relationship with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, to the US trade blacklist.

Trump blasted the new leadership of CBS News’ 60 Minutes, which was overhauled under the network’s conservative editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. In a social media post, the president was particularly critical of a report on the more than 800 American service members wounded and 23 killed in the war in Iran that 60 Minutes aired on Sunday.

⁠Trump also said that he ⁠would “not mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. The president says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denied that national security has been put at risk.

The president also continued to shift responsibility to the Biden administration for the nationwide ground stop over the weekend. Trump said that he needed more funding to overhaul the outdated telecommunication system responsible for the disruptions.

The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren, the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, that she could face “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump. The warning mirrors other letters justice department officials have sent to Democratic lawmakers who have indicated they will investigate the Trump administration when the party becomes the majority in Congress next year.

A federal appeals court heard arguments in Donald Trump’s hush money case, as the president tries to see the case shifted to federal court where he could have it dismissed on grounds of immunity. The hearing concerned a May 2024 ruling that found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.

Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
Blake Montgomery and Johana Bhuiyan
Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday, after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.
The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him.

In a new memoir, Joe Biden offers harsh criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has led Ukraine through four-and-a-half years of war against Russia. According to Biden, the Ukrainian president was “difficult to work with”, “moody and stubborn in our private conversations”, and “not as grateful as I expected” for US diplomatic support and military aid.

Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, was published on Tuesday, shortly before his 84th birthday and as he battles advanced prostate cancer. Largely a trumpeting of achievements in office, with scant admission of failings ultimately crowned by his own party deeming him unfit for office and forcing his withdrawal from the 2024 campaign against Donald Trump, the book has not been well reviewed.

The war in Ukraine takes up much of the middle of the book. Detailing frustrating talks with Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, Biden describes the buildup to war and US-Ukraine co-operation from the invasion of February 2022 until Biden left office in January 2025.
His portrait of Zelenskyy is not entirely negative.

“I had worried that President Zelenskyy, who had come from such an unlikely background [as a comedian and actor] might not have the right stuff for a crisis like this one,” Biden writes. “This was no TV comedy.” But, the former president adds, he found himself impressed by Zelenskyy’s fortitude, and “delighted that my worries proved to be unfounded”.

At a press conference earlier, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, pledged to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, restore Medicaid cuts, expand Medicare eligibility, end “the reckless and costly war of choice” on Iran, end tariffs, and end Citizens United.
“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he said.

He also called for banning members of Congress from trading stocks, saying: “That will be a high priority. This is what the American people are demanding that we do, and we are going to execute on that mission.”

Jeffries was speaking ahead of the vote tomorrow to elect the next House speaker, which he is expected to win. Asked about progressive resistance to making him speaker, Jeffries replied: “You’ll have to ask, you know, those individuals that you believe are resistant to voting for me in caucus tomorrow.”
Can Chris Van Hollen really beat Chuck Schumer? – podcast

The blue wave has hit Washington, and with the flood of new Democratic lawmakers comes a debate over who should lead the party. Yesterday, Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen said his campaign to unseat Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader is gathering momentum. He has painted himself as the underdog candidate to Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade. What does this leadership battle tell us about the kind of party Democrats want to be?

In today’s episode of our Stateside podcast, Kai Wright speaks to the Guardian’s senior politics reporter Chris Stein about Van Hollen’s chances, and hears from the Guardian’s midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang about why new senators in her region are having doubts about Schumer.
Senators set to vote on controversial nominee to lead FDA

Lawmakers in the Senate health, labor and pensions committee are set to vote on Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Wednesday. A reminder that the FDA is the body that oversees US approvals for prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs and vaccines, as well as much of the country’s food supply.

Overton has received bipartisan pushback to head up the agency, which sits within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). During a confirmation hearing in September, she faced questions from Republican and Democratic lawmakers about her stance on vaccines. While she said that “every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective”, Overton gave evasive answers about how she would push back against Donald Trump and his administration when they undermine trust in vaccines at a time when the US is experiencing the highest number of measles cases in decades (the US has since lost its measles elimination status).

Overton also did not correct the president’s statement that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) could be “quite lethal” during an executive order announcement about revisions to the childhood vaccine schedule. This despite the scientific consensus that inoculation is the best method of prevention for all three viruses.
At the time, Senator Bill Cassidy, the health committee’s Republican chair, said Overton’s “active role” in the directive was “almost disqualifying”.

On Sunday, Cassidy told CBS News that he remained uncertain about Overton’s path to confirmation. “I still have questions. And so, I cannot tell you the outcome of that vote right now,” the outgoing senator said.

“We’re not going to have perfection,” Cassidy added. “The question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody’s mind but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence,”

If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A former physician, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term.
Hung Cao faces lawmakers to become permanent Navy secretary as Iran war continues
Hung Cao, who currently serves as the acting Navy secretary, is facing lawmakers on the Senate armed services committee to be confirmed as the permanent top official.

However, in order to be confirmed Cao will need 60 votes for a congressional waiver to exempt him from the federal law that requires former military officers to have been retired from active-duty service for at least seven years before they are eligible to take top civilian Pentagon positions.
Since Cao only retired as a Navy captain in 2021, he’ll need at least seven Democrats to cross the aisle and confirm him, compared to the usual simple majority required for a presidential nomination.
Jensen Huang agrees to appear before House lawmakers in wake of Nvidia scandal

Jensen Huang, the embattled former CEO of Nvidia, will appear before House lawmakers on the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews on 1 December.
Huang will appear alongside Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the Republican chairs of the respective committees. Huang’s testimony will come after he resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia last week following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Her company, Megaspeed, was under investigation for purchasing Nvidia’s advanced chips and allegedly diverting them to China.

While the battle between Democrats Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer continues for Senate majority leader in the new Congress, in the House Hakeem Jeffries is still poised to clinch role of Speaker, making history as the first Black member to lead the lower chamber.
As of now, there doesn’t seem to be any clear opposition to Jeffries’ bid. Last week, the long-serving Democratic congressman Glenn Ivey told me on the phone that Jeffries is “a shoo-in”.
“I don’t even know if he’ll have any competition. It could well be done by acclamation [voice vote]. I guess we’ll just have to see,” he added.

Today, however, Punchbowl News reported that Jeffries instead plans to ask for a recorded vote in the Democratic caucus meeting on Wednesday, as a sign that he is not worried about the numbers he has to win.

A reminder that while the election for Senate leadership happens in a closed-door, secret ballot, the House Speaker is elected by the entire chamber in the new year. As of now, Democrats have an 85-seat majority in the House, with 18 races yet to be called.
National Security Agency highly classified network goes down - report
The highly classified network that the national security agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to a report by CNN, citing six people familiar with the matter.

NSA Net, the network, allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally. According to CNN’s sources, there is no evidence of a cyber-attack, but the NSA has now launched staggered arrivals of their staff.
The Guardian has contacted the NSA for comment.

In lighter news today, new members in the US House are all taking part in the time honored tradition of the suite selection lottery, where every incoming representative has the chance to snag one of the available offices for the new Congress.
